result.markdown: --- title: "Session 5 — More Groups, Repeated Measures, Correlation and Reporting" subtitle: "One-way and Welch ANOVA · Kruskal–Wallis · repeated measures and sphericity · Friedman · post hoc tests · Pearson and Spearman · multiple testing · Lab 5" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Session 4: two groups, or two measurements on the same people - Today: **three or more** groups or time points, the **relationship** between two numbers, and putting it all into **words** - By the end you can: - run ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis, and their **post hoc** tests, only when they are warranted - check **sphericity** for repeated measures and use **paired** post hoc tests - read **r**, its CI and **r²**, and choose Pearson or Spearman - control for **multiple testing**, and write a results paragraph ::: # Topic 1 — Three or more independent groups {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## One-way ANOVA: height by marital status ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> group_by(marital_status_of_participants) |> summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(height), sd = sd(height)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 marital_status_of_participants n mean sd 1 never married 134 173. 10.6 2 currently married 401 170. 10.8 3 formerly/ever married 96 170. 10.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} a_h <- aov(height ~ marital_status_of_participants, data = p) summary(a_h) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) marital_status_of_participants 2 664 332 2.887 0.0565 . Residuals 628 72209 115 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Check the assumptions on the residuals ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s5_groups_correlation_reporting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=460} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} leveneTest(height ~ marital_status_of_participants, data = p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median) Df F value Pr(>F) group 2 0.1775 0.8374 628 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} oneway.test(height ~ marital_status_of_participants, data = p)$p.value # Welch ANOVA ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.05646725 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: - Residuals on the line, similar SDs (Levene p = 0.837), and **Welch ANOVA** agrees: the classical ANOVA is fine ## A borderline result: read it, do not round it ::: {.eq} "Mean height differed little by marital status: 172.5 cm in never married, 170.1 in currently married and 169.9 in formerly married adults (one-way ANOVA, F(2, 628) = 2.89, p = 0.056; η² = 0.009)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - p = 0.056 is **not** "nearly significant" or "a trend": it is weak evidence, and η² says marital status explains under **1%** of the variation in height - The largest difference (never vs currently married) is 2.5 cm, 95% CI -0.03 to 5.00 (Tukey): compatible with **no** difference and with a few cm ::: ## Post hoc tests: when and which | After | Post hoc | R | |---|---|---| | One-way ANOVA, equal SDs | **Tukey HSD** | `TukeyHSD(aov(...))` | | Welch ANOVA, unequal SDs | **Games–Howell** | `rstatix::games_howell_test()` | | Kruskal–Wallis | **Dunn** with Holm adjustment | `rstatix::dunn_test(..., p.adjust.method = "holm")` | ::: {.warn} Run post hoc tests to answer a question you **planned**, or after a clear overall result. Hunting through every pair after a non-significant overall test produces false findings. ::: ## Kruskal–Wallis: systolic pressure by marital status ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> group_by(marital_status_of_participants) |> summarise(median = median(sbp_presentation), q1 = quantile(sbp_presentation, .25), q3 = quantile(sbp_presentation, .75)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 marital_status_of_participants median q1 q3 1 never married 153 128 189 2 currently married 151 125 182 3 formerly/ever married 149 122. 174. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} kruskal.test(sbp_presentation ~ marital_status_of_participants, data = p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test data: sbp_presentation by marital_status_of_participants Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 1.1131, df = 2, p-value = 0.5732 ``` ::: ::: - For skewed outcomes or outliers (SBP has implausible values, Session 1); compares the **distributions**, through ranks - p = 0.573 and almost identical medians: **no** evidence of a difference, so **no** post hoc tests # Topic 2 — Repeated measurements {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Repeated-measures ANOVA: fasting glucose at 0, 3 and 6 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fbs_long <- p |> select(s_no, fbs_presentation, fbs_3_months, fbs_6_months) |> pivot_longer(-s_no, names_to = "time", values_to = "fbs") anova_test(data = fbs_long, dv = fbs, wid = s_no, within = time) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ANOVA Table (type III tests) $ANOVA Effect DFn DFd F p p<.05 ges 1 time 2 1260 360.517 1.55e-124 * 0.281 $`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity` Effect W p p<.05 1 time 1 0.858 $`Sphericity Corrections` Effect GGe DF[GG] p[GG] p[GG]<.05 HFe DF[HF] p[HF] 1 time 1 2, 1259.39 1.78e-124 * 1.003 2.01, 1263.39 1.55e-124 p[HF]<.05 1 * ``` ::: ::: ## Sphericity, and the correction ::: {.incremental} - **Sphericity**: the variance of the differences is the same for every pair of time points (0–3, 0–6, 3–6) - **Mauchly's test** checks it; when violated, use the **Greenhouse–Geisser** corrected p-value (`p[GG]`), which `anova_test()` prints alongside - Here Mauchly p = 0.858 and the GG ε ≈ 1.00: no problem - **ges** (generalised η²) = 0.28: time explains a large share of the variation ::: ::: {.eq} "Mean fasting glucose fell from 100.2 mg/dL at presentation to 90.1 at 3 and 85.0 at 6 months (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(2, 1260) = 361, p < 0.001; generalised η² = 0.28)." ::: ## Post hoc for repeated measures must be **paired** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairwise.t.test(fbs_long$fbs, fbs_long$time, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pairwise comparisons using paired t tests data: fbs_long$fbs and fbs_long$time fbs_3_months fbs_6_months fbs_6_months <2e-16 - fbs_presentation <2e-16 <2e-16 P value adjustment method: bonferroni ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} Without `paired = TRUE`, `pairwise.t.test()` treats the three visits as **independent groups** of different people and pools their SD: the wrong test for repeated measurements. Here every change is large, so the p-values agree; with smaller changes the unpaired version can miss or invent a difference. ::: ## Friedman: systolic pressure at 0, 3 and 6 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sbp_long <- p |> select(s_no, sbp_presentation, sbp_3_months, sbp_6_months) |> pivot_longer(-s_no, names_to = "time", values_to = "sbp") friedman.test(sbp ~ time | s_no, data = sbp_long) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Friedman rank sum test data: sbp and time and s_no Friedman chi-squared = 140.12, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pairwise.wilcox.test(sbp_long$sbp, sbp_long$time, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm")$p.value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sbp_3_months sbp_6_months sbp_6_months 7.990284e-06 NA sbp_presentation 1.032414e-15 1.593068e-38 ``` ::: ::: - The rank-based partner of repeated-measures ANOVA; every person needs **all** time points - Medians 151 → 133 → 121 mmHg; effect size **Kendall's W** = 0.11 (0.1 small, 0.3 moderate, 0.5 large) # Topic 3 — Two numbers together: correlation {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Plot first, then r ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s5_groups_correlation_reporting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=500} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cor.test(p$age_of_participants, p$sbp_in_mm_hg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's product-moment correlation data: p$age_of_participants and p$sbp_in_mm_hg t = 4.4791, df = 629, p-value = 8.903e-06 alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 0.09912043 0.25042775 sample estimates: cor 0.1758122 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Reading r ::: {.eq} "Systolic pressure rose slightly with age (Pearson r = 0.18, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.25; p < 0.001)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - **r²** = 0.03: age accounts for about **3%** of the variation in SBP. Highly significant, yet **weak** - Correlation measures **linear association** only; it is not agreement (use Bland–Altman for that) and not causation - To estimate *how much* SBP changes per year of age, and to adjust for other factors: **regression** (Regression track) ::: ## Pearson or Spearman? | | Pearson r | Spearman ρ | |---|---|---| | Measures | **linear** association | **monotonic** association (through ranks) | | Needs | roughly normal pairs, no extreme outliers | ordinal or numeric data, any shape | | Use for | age and SBP | glucose (skewed, outliers up to 487 mg/dL), ordinal scores | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cor.test(p$age_of_participants, p$glucose_level_mg_d_l, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)$estimate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rho 0.1130115 ``` ::: ::: # Topic 4 — Many tests, and the write-up {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Multiple testing ::: {.incremental} - At p < 0.05, **1 in 20** tests of a true null hypothesis comes out "significant" by chance - 20 independent comparisons → about a **64%** chance of at least one false positive - **Bonferroni**: multiply each p by the number of tests (simple, strict). **Holm**: the same idea step by step, never worse, usually better - `p.adjust(c(0.01, 0.02, 0.04), method = "holm")` → 0.03, 0.04, 0.04 - Decide the **main** comparisons in advance; label the rest as **exploratory** ::: ## A results paragraph ::: {.eq} "Of 631 adults, 34 (5.4%) reported diabetes. They were older (mean difference 8.9 years, 95% CI 4.1 to 13.7; Welch t-test) and more often hypertensive (odds ratio 9.2, 95% CI 4.0 to 20.7; Fisher's exact test). Mean fasting glucose fell over six months (Topic 2)." ::: - **Every** claim: the numbers, the **effect with its CI**, the **test**; p-values to 2–3 decimals, "p < 0.001" below that - Methods: how assumptions were checked and what was done when they failed (Session 2) ## Reporting checklist | | Write down | |---|---| | Descriptives | n for every group; mean (SD) or median (IQR); n (%) | | Data checks | what was excluded and why; sensitivity analysis | | Assumptions | how checked (plots, tests); what was done if not met | | Each result | effect size **with 95% CI**, the test, the exact p | | Many tests | which were planned; the adjustment method | | Interpretation | size and importance, not only "significant"; association, not cause | ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 5 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `stats-workshop/labs/lab5_more_groups.R` - one-way ANOVA with residual checks, Welch ANOVA and Tukey - Kruskal–Wallis, and when not to run post hoc tests - repeated-measures ANOVA with sphericity, and **paired** post hoc tests - Friedman with Kendall's W - Pearson and Spearman, r², and a Holm adjustment ::: **Time:** 40 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t5q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="sbshws.lmnrbg" data-show="V2VhayBldmlkZW5jZSwgYW5kIHRoZSBncm91cGluZyBleHBsYWlucyB1bmRlciAxJSBvZiB2 YXJpYXRpb24=" data-explain="cCA9IDAuMDU2IGlzIHdlYWsgZXZpZGVuY2UsIG5vdCBhICd0cmVuZCc7IGV0YSBzcXVhcmVk IGJlbG93IDAuMDEgbWVhbnMgdGhlIGdyb3VwaW5nIGV4cGxhaW5zIGFsbW9zdCBub25lIG9m IHRoZSB2YXJpYXRpb24uIFJlcG9ydCB0aGUgZ3JvdXAgbWVhbnMgYW5kIHRoZSBDSXMu"} A one-way ANOVA gives p = 0.056 and eta squared = 0.009. What is the best reading? - A trend that would be significant with a few more people - Weak evidence, and the grouping explains under 1% of variation - Clear evidence of a difference, since p is close to 0.05 - The groups are now proven equal, so no differences are reported ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t5q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="sbsv5h.lmo5st" data-show="cGFpcndpc2UudC50ZXN0KCkgd2l0aCBwYWlyZWQgPSBUUlVFIGFuZCBhbiBhZGp1c3RtZW50 " data-explain="VGhlIHNhbWUgcGVvcGxlIGFwcGVhciBhdCBldmVyeSB0aW1lIHBvaW50LCBzbyB0aGUgY29t cGFyaXNvbnMgbXVzdCBiZSBwYWlyZWQsIHdpdGggYSBjb3JyZWN0aW9uIChCb25mZXJyb25p IG9yIEhvbG0pIGZvciB0aGUgdGhyZWUgdGVzdHMu"} Fasting glucose was measured in the same adults at 0, 3 and 6 months. Which post hoc comparison is right after a repeated-measures ANOVA? - pairwise.t.test() with the default settings on the long data - pairwise.t.test() with paired = TRUE and an adjustment - Three separate Welch t-tests with no multiplicity adjustment - A Tukey HSD test on the aov() of glucose by time point only ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t5q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="sbt8e7.lmoka7" data-show="VGhlIEdyZWVuaG91c2UtR2Vpc3NlciBjb3JyZWN0ZWQgcC12YWx1ZSBmb3IgdGhlIHRpbWUg ZWZmZWN0" data-explain="QSBzbWFsbCBNYXVjaGx5IHAgbWVhbnMgc3BoZXJpY2l0eSBpcyB2aW9sYXRlZC4gVGhlIEdy ZWVuaG91c2UtR2Vpc3NlciBjb3JyZWN0aW9uIGFkanVzdHMgdGhlIGRlZ3JlZXMgb2YgZnJl ZWRvbTsgYW5vdmFfdGVzdCgpIHByaW50cyBpdCBhcyBwW0dHXS4="} Mauchly's test for a repeated-measures ANOVA gives p = 0.002. What should you report? - The uncorrected F-test, since sphericity is a minor point - A Kruskal-Wallis test in place of the repeated measures model - The Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-value for the time effect - Nothing, as the analysis cannot be done with these data ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t5q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="sbtlmv.lmoyrj" data-show="QWdlIGV4cGxhaW5zIGFib3V0IDMlIG9mIHRoZSB2YXJpYXRpb24gaW4gU0JQ" data-explain="ciBzcXVhcmVkID0gMC4wMzogYSByZWFsIGJ1dCB3ZWFrIGFzc29jaWF0aW9uLiBBIHNtYWxs IHAgcmVmbGVjdHMgdGhlIGxhcmdlIHNhbXBsZSwgbm90IHN0cmVuZ3RoLiBDb3JyZWxhdGlv biBpcyBuZWl0aGVyIGNhdXNhdGlvbiBub3IgYWdyZWVtZW50Lg=="} Age and systolic pressure: r = 0.18, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.25, p < 0.001. What is the right reading? - A strong link, since the p-value is so very small - Age explains about 3% of the variation in SBP - Getting older causes a rise in systolic pressure - SBP and age agree closely when measured in adults ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t5q5" data-type="fill" data-hashes="hg746j.fmd9bs,cyahie.972xex,rbx6ny.gnf7dl,hg746k.fmd9bt,rk0h4s.gwo9u3" data-show="NjQ=" data-explain="MSAtIDAuOTVeMjAgPSAwLjY0LiBQbGFuIHRoZSBtYWluIGNvbXBhcmlzb25zLCBhZGp1c3Qg KEhvbG0gb3IgQm9uZmVycm9uaSksIGFuZCBsYWJlbCB0aGUgcmVzdCBhcyBleHBsb3JhdG9y eS4="} With 20 independent tests at the 5% level and every null hypothesis true, the chance of at least one false positive is about what percent? (number only) ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - ≥ 3 groups: ANOVA (Welch if SDs differ) or **Kruskal–Wallis**; post hoc only when warranted - Repeated measures: check **sphericity**; post hoc tests must be **paired** - Correlation: **plot**, then r with its CI; r² for strength; not cause, not agreement - Plan the main tests; **adjust** the rest; report effect sizes with CIs, in sentences ::: **Next:** the **Regression** track: the same questions with several factors at once

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
